chunks: Thin coil wire versus high current. The question: Motor/solenoids often require many loops in the coils, so the coil wires will be very thin.
Motors/solenoids also draw lots of current, possibly more than the coils can support. How do you reconcile this? Do coils on the motors always burn out?
It sounds as if a coil of many thin turns must carry a big current, but it is the reverse.
More turns of thinner wire means more resistance, so at a given voltage the current is smaller.
A coil's force depends on ampere-turns, which is the number of turns times the current. Designers choose the number of turns to fit the supply voltage.
Big currents appear only at start-up, stall, or overload. Coils burn out only when heat outruns cooling.
Think of pushing water through a garden hose. A longer, thinner hose lets less water through at the same pressure.
Winding more turns of thinner wire is like swapping in a longer, narrower hose: the flow (current) drops sharply.
To get the same push from the coil, you pair that long thin hose with a higher-pressure supply.
With heat dissipation fixed at 0. 54 watts, current falls as 1 over V ( I equals P over V ). Higher supply voltage means more turns of thinner wire carrying less current.
In every case the ampere-turns are 200 and the current density is 4 amps/mm².
Ampere-turns ( NI ): turns times current. It sets how strongly a coil magnetizes. Current density ( J ): current per square millimeter of wire. It sets the heating.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates against the supply. It cuts the running current. Duty cycle: the fraction of time a solenoid may stay energized.
Take a coil with room for about 2 cm³ of copper and a limit of 4 amps/mm². The copper fills a 50 mm² cross-section, so 4 amps/mm² allows 200 ampere-turns.
On 5 volts you wind about 1860 turns, which draws about 108 milliamps. On 12 volts you wind about 4460 turns of thinner wire, which draws about 45 milliamps.
Both make 200 ampere-turns. At 4 amps/mm², copper heats at only about 0. 08 degrees Celsius per second.
At 20 amps/mm² it heats at about 2 degrees Celsius per second, so a stall heats the coil 100 degrees Celsius in under a minute. That is the whole idea.

12 mm wire draws about 45 milliamps at 12 volts.
Large currents occur only at start, stall or overload; a running motor's back-EMF limits current, and solenoids are rated by duty cycle.
Coils don't always burn out; they fail when heat outruns cooling, so designers hold current density to a few amps per square millimetre and protect against stall."
